project.title: DevBlog: Secure Blog REST API with JWT, Roles and AI Moderation
project.tagline: Build a secure, production-style blogging backend from requirements to monitoring, with AI as your pair programmer
project.description: Over nine phases you build DevBlog like a professional team: requirements, design, a test-first implementation of JWT auth with refresh-token rotation, role-based access, posts with optimistic locking, keyset pagination and full-text search, comments with AI moderation and a human in the loop, CI/CD with GitHub Actions, Docker, optional free-tier deployment, observability and a retrospective. Pick Java, Python or TypeScript; the spec, database and tests are shared. Everything runs on your laptop, and the AI features work offline.

Design a REST API contract-first (OpenAPI) with a PostgreSQL schema and ADRs
Implement authentication properly: bcrypt, short-lived JWTs, rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection
Enforce roles and ownership, optimistic locking, keyset pagination and full-text search
Add AI comment moderation that only holds comments for a human and falls back offline
Build CI/CD with GitHub Actions: matrix, caching, reusable workflows, service containers, GHCR
Add request IDs, JSON logs, metrics and a circuit breaker after a game day and a blameless post-mortem
Use AI assistants deliberately and verify every output

phases.title: Setup and orientation
phases.heading: Phase 0 · Setup and orientation
phases.why_md:
Every professional project starts with a working local environment and a clean Git workflow. Teams
lose days to "works on my machine". In this phase you set up the tools for **one** track, run the
starter, meet the test suite that will guide you, open your first pull request and start your
`AI_LOG.md`. That is the evidence a reviewer looks for first: a repo that builds from a clean checkout
with one command.
objectives: Fork the repository **with all branches and tags**, clone it and add the `upstream` remote.
Pick a track (Java, Python or TypeScript) and install its toolchain on Windows (WSL2), macOS or Linux.
Start PostgreSQL with Docker Compose and run the starter so `GET /health` returns `UP`.
Run lint and tests locally and see which tests are *pending* and why.
Open a pull request that passes CI and write your first `AI_LOG.md` entry.

steps.title: Fork and clone (keep the tags!)
steps.content_md:
1. On GitHub open `AICanCode-org/blog-rest-api` → **Fork**. **Untick "Copy the `main` branch only"**.
   The `solution` branch and the `phase-N-end` tags are your safety net in later phases.
2. Clone **your** fork and connect the original as `upstream`:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<you>/blog-rest-api.git
   cd blog-rest-api
   git remote add upstream https://github.com/AICanCode-org/blog-rest-api.git
   git fetch upstream --tags
   git tag -l 'phase-*'      # you should see phase-0-end … phase-8-end
   ```
3. **Windows:** do all of this inside **WSL2** (Ubuntu) and keep the repo in the Linux file system
   (`~/code/blog-rest-api`), not under `/mnt/c`. File watching and Docker volumes are 5–10× faster there.

steps.title: Install Docker and the tools for ONE track
steps.content_md:
* **All tracks:** Git, Docker (Docker Desktop on Windows/macOS with the WSL2 backend; Docker Engine +
  compose plugin on Linux), `make` and `curl`.
* Then run the doctor script. It tells you exactly what is missing:
  ```bash
  scripts/doctor.sh
  ```

<!-- track:java -->
**Java track:** JDK 21 (Temurin) and Maven 3.9+. The easiest way on Linux/macOS/WSL is SDKMAN:
```bash
curl -s https://get.sdkman.io | bash   # then open a new terminal
sdk install java 21-tem && sdk install maven
java -version && mvn -v
```
<!-- /track -->

macOS: `brew install python@3.12`).
```bash

cd tracks/python && make install     # creates .venv and installs pinned dependencies
```

steps.title: Start the database
steps.content_md:
```bash
docker compose up -d postgres
docker compose ps          # postgres should be "healthy"
```
The first start also creates a second database, `devblog_test`, that the integration tests use
(`spec/db/init/01-create-test-db.sql`), so tests can never wipe your dev data. Port 5432 already taken
(another Postgres)? Set `POSTGRES_PORT=55432` in `.env` and use that port in `DATABASE_URL`.

steps.content_md:
<!-- track:java -->
```bash

make run                   # mvn spring-boot:run, listens on :8080
```
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
```bash

```
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
```bash

make run                   # tsx watch src/index.ts, listens on :8080
```

In another terminal:
```bash
curl -s localhost:8080/health
# {"status":"UP","checks":{"database":"UP"}}
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/auth/register -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
# {"type":"https://devblog.example/problems/internal-error","title":"Internal server error","status":500}
```
The endpoints already exist, but they answer `500` because the business logic is a `TODO`: that is
Phase 3. Notice that even the crash is a clean `application/problem+json` body with no stack trace:

`make run` sets **local-only** defaults for `JWT_SECRET` and the first admin (`admin@devblog.local`). They
are fine on your laptop and wrong anywhere else; Phase 6 shows how a deployment sets its own.

steps.title: Run the checks and meet the pending tests
steps.content_md:
```bash
make lint test
```
You will see **a few passing tests** (`/health`, and in Java the `DATABASE_URL` parser) and well over a
hundred **skipped** ones. They are *pending*: the complete test suite for DevBlog is already written and
switched off in one file per track:

| Track | Pending list |
|---|---|
| Java | `tracks/java/src/test/java/org/aicancode/devblog/support/Pending.java` |
| Python | `tracks/python/tests/conftest.py` (`PENDING`) |
| TypeScript | `tracks/typescript/test/pending.ts` (`PENDING`) |

Open the list now. Each entry names a milestone ("Phase 3 M2 - auth endpoints"). In Phase 3 you delete
one entry at a time, watch the tests go red, and make them green.

steps.title: Your first pull request
steps.content_md:
1. Create a branch: `git switch -c chore/phase-0-setup`.
2. Fill in the first entry in `AI_LOG.md`, e.g. how an assistant helped you install the toolchain and
   how you checked its advice.
3. Commit and push, then open a PR **in your fork** against your `main`:
   ```bash
   git add AI_LOG.md
   git commit -m "docs: start AI_LOG for phase 0"
   git push -u origin chore/phase-0-setup
   ```
4. Open the **Actions** tab. Forks have Actions switched off until you click **"I understand my
   workflows, go ahead and enable them"**. The CI workflow runs lint + unit tests for all three tracks.
   Wait for green, fill in the PR template and merge.

ai_prompts.title: Fix my toolchain install
ai_prompts.prompt:
I'm on <Windows 11 + WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 | macOS 15 | Ubuntu 24.04>. I want to run a <Java 21 + Maven |
Python 3.12 | Node 22> project with Docker Compose. Here is the output of scripts/doctor.sh:
<paste output>. Give me the exact commands to install what is missing, explain each one in one line,
and tell me how to verify each install.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: running each verification command it gives you, re-running `scripts/doctor.sh` until every line is green, and checking any download URL against the official site (adoptium.net, python.org, nodejs.org, docker.com). Never pipe an unknown URL into `bash`.

ai_prompts.title: Explain the starter
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is the file tree of a starter project and the file <tracks/<track>/…/main entry file>:
<paste>. Explain in plain English what happens from "make run" until GET /health returns, which
files are involved, where environment variables are read, and where an unexpected exception is turned
into an HTTP 500 response. Do not suggest code changes.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: finding each file and function it names (an assistant may invent ones that do not exist), then changing `PORT=8081 make run` to confirm the app really listens on the new port.

ai_prompts.title: What will I build?
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is an OpenAPI 3.1 contract: <paste spec/openapi.yaml>. Summarise in 10 bullet points what this
API does, which endpoints need authentication, which need a specific role, and which three endpoints
you expect to be the hardest to get right. Quote the path for every claim.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: checking every quoted path and `security`/role note against the file. Mark anything it got wrong; you will meet the same contract in Phases 2 and 3.

quiz.q: Why must you untick "Copy the main branch only" when forking?
options: Otherwise GitHub Actions is disabled in the fork
Otherwise the `solution` branch and phase tags are missing from your fork
Otherwise you cannot open pull requests
Otherwise Docker Compose cannot find the database
quiz.explanation: Forks copy only `main` by default. The tags (`phase-N-end`) live on the `solution` branch; without them you cannot compare your work or catch up. Fix it later with `git fetch upstream --tags`.

quiz.q: On Windows, where should the repository live?
options: Inside the WSL2 Linux file system, e.g. `~/code/blog-rest-api`
On a network drive so Docker can share it
quiz.explanation: Cross-file-system access from WSL to `/mnt/c` is slow and breaks file watching. Keep code in the Linux file system and open it with VS Code's WSL extension.

quiz.q: Why do integration tests use a separate `devblog_test` database?
options: PostgreSQL allows only one connection per database
The tests empty the tables before each test, which must never touch your dev data
quiz.explanation: Integration tests truncate tables to start from a known state. A separate database (created by `spec/db/init`) makes that safe on your laptop.

quiz.q: Why are most tests skipped in the starter?
options: CI is too slow to run them
They describe behaviour you will implement in Phases 3–4 and are switched on one milestone at a time
They only run on the solution branch
quiz.explanation: The full suite is written up-front (a test-first workflow). Deleting a line from the pending list turns a group back on, so you always have a clear red → green target.

quiz.q: Which of these should never go into an AI prompt?
options: A stack trace from your own code
Your `.env` file with the JWT secret and API keys
quiz.explanation: Secrets and personal data never go into prompts. Anyone with the JWT secret can mint an ADMIN token for your API. Redact before you paste.

quiz.q: The starter answers `500` for `POST /api/v1/auth/register`. Why is the body still JSON without a stack trace?
options: The framework hides errors in production mode automatically
The starter already maps unexpected exceptions to a generic `problem+json` response and logs the details server-side
The endpoint is not implemented in the router
quiz.explanation: Leaking stack traces tells attackers your stack and file layout. Clients get a generic problem body; the details go to the server log.

recap: A reproducible local environment: Docker Compose for the database, one toolchain per track.
The difference between `origin` (your fork) and `upstream` (the course repo), and why tags matter.
How a health check reports its dependency, and that errors are a clean, generic contract.
Pending tests as a to-do list: the spec is executable before you write any code.
The PR + CI loop and the habit of logging AI assistance without leaking secrets.

phases.title: Requirements, threats and user stories
phases.heading: Phase 1 · Requirements, threats and user stories
phases.why_md:
Most failed projects fail before the first line of code: nobody wrote down what "done" means. For an
API with logins and roles there is a second question that teams skip until it hurts: **what could go
wrong?** A short, testable requirements document with an explicit threat list gives every test a
reason to exist, lets you say *no* to scope creep, and is the first thing an interviewer asks about.
AI assistants are great at drafting requirements, and just as good at inventing requirements nobody
asked for. Your job is to keep the ones you can test.
objectives: Turn a one-paragraph brief into numbered **functional** (FR) and **measurable non-functional** (NFR) requirements.
Map personas to **roles** (READER, AUTHOR, ADMIN) and write down who may do what.
List at least five **threats** (abuse cases) and the requirement that answers each.
Write 8–10 **user stories** with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and create them as GitHub Issues.
Write an explicit **out-of-scope** list and a **back-of-the-envelope estimate**.

steps.title: Read the brief and the contract
steps.content_md:
> *Build DevBlog: the backend of a small multi-author blog for a student tech club. Anyone can read
> published posts, search them and filter by tag. Registered members comment. Authors write Markdown
> posts as drafts and publish when ready. Admins promote members to authors and review comments that
> an AI flagged. It must run on a laptop for free, work without any AI service, and be safe enough that
> a member cannot read drafts, edit someone else's post or make themselves admin.*

Open `spec/openapi.yaml`. The HTTP contract is **given** so the three tracks stay compatible; your
requirements must be consistent with it (status codes, limits, the `problem+json` error format, which
endpoints declare `security: bearerAuth`).

steps.title: Personas and the permission matrix
steps.content_md:
Write at least three personas (e.g. *Ravi, a reader on his phone*; *Meera, a second-year student who
writes tutorials*; *Arjun, the club admin*). Then fill a matrix: rows = actions (read published post,
read a draft, create post, edit own post, edit any post, comment, delete own comment, moderate,
change roles), columns = anonymous, READER, AUTHOR, ADMIN. Every "no" in this table becomes a test in
Phase 3. Decide now what a refused request returns: `401` (not logged in), `403` (logged in, not
allowed) or `404` (you should not even learn that it exists, e.g. someone else's draft).

steps.title: Functional requirements
steps.content_md:
In `spec/requirements.md` write FR-1 … FR-n as "The system shall …" statements. Each needs a number
or a status code, so a test can check it. Bad: *"Passwords must be secure."* Good: *"Passwords are 8–72
bytes and stored only as bcrypt hashes with cost ≥ 10."* Cover registration, login, refresh, logout,
roles, posts (drafts, publish, edit, delete), the feed (pagination, tags, search), comments,
moderation, summaries and health.

steps.title: Non-functional requirements and threats
steps.content_md:
Cover security, performance, availability, privacy, cost and portability. Make each one measurable:
*"access tokens expire after 15 minutes"*, *"the feed answers in < 100 ms p95 with 10 000 posts on a
laptop"*, *"comments can still be posted when the LLM is down"*.

Then the threat list. For each abuse case, name the requirement that stops it:

| Threat | Answer |
|---|---|
| A stolen refresh token is used by an attacker | rotation + reuse detection (FR-3) |
| A new user sends `"role":"ADMIN"` when registering | registration ignores `role` (FR-1) |
| Someone guesses the slug of a draft | drafts are `404` for others (FR-7) |
| Two authors edit the same post and one change silently disappears | optimistic locking (FR-8) |
| Spam floods the comments | moderation holds it for a human (FR-12, FR-13) |

steps.title: User stories → GitHub Issues
steps.content_md:
For each story use the **User story** issue template (`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/user_story.yml`). It asks
for the story, the acceptance criteria and the Phase 3 milestone. Label them `user-story`. With the
GitHub CLI:
```bash
gh issue create --template user_story.yml      # or use the web UI: Issues → New issue
```
Write at least one acceptance criterion per story that describes a **refusal** (wrong role, wrong
owner, bad input), not only the happy path.

steps.title: Out of scope + estimates
steps.content_md:
List what v1 will **not** do (front end, image upload, e-mail verification, password reset, OAuth,
likes, rate limiting…). Then estimate: authors, posts/day, reads/day, comments/day, read:write ratio,
requests/second at peak (× 10 of average) and storage per year. Write one sentence on what the numbers
mean for the design (spoiler: one PostgreSQL instance is plenty; the hard part is correctness, not scale).

steps.title: Commit
steps.content_md:
```bash
git switch -c docs/phase-1-requirements
git add spec/requirements.md AI_LOG.md
git commit -m "docs(spec): requirements, threats and user stories"
git push -u origin docs/phase-1-requirements      # open a PR, wait for CI, merge
```
Compare with the reference: `git diff phase-0-end phase-1-end -- spec/requirements.md`.

ai_prompts.title: Draft requirements from the brief
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is a product brief: <paste the brief> and an OpenAPI contract: <paste spec/openapi.yaml>.
Draft numbered functional requirements ("The system shall ...") and measurable non-functional
requirements for v1. Every requirement must be testable and consistent with the contract (quote the
status code or limit). Do not add features that are not in the brief or the contract.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: checking every number and status code against `spec/openapi.yaml`, deleting anything not in the brief (AI loves adding e-mail verification and OAuth), and asking "which test would prove this?" for each line. If you cannot name the test, rewrite or drop it.

ai_prompts.title: Threat-model the API
ai_prompts.prompt:
Act as a security reviewer. For this API (contract: <paste>) with roles READER, AUTHOR and ADMIN and
JWT access tokens + refresh tokens, list the 8 most likely abuse cases for a small public blog. For
each: the attack in one sentence, the impact, and a concrete, testable countermeasure. Prefer
OWASP API Security Top 10 categories and name them.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: looking up each named OWASP API Top 10 category on owasp.org (assistants sometimes misname them), keeping only threats that apply to *this* contract, and making sure each kept countermeasure appears as an FR or NFR.

ai_prompts.title: Turn my stories into Given/When/Then
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here are my user stories: <paste>. For each, write 2-4 acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then form,
including at least one refusal case (wrong role, someone else's resource, invalid input). Use only
status codes from this contract: <paste the relevant paths>.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: cross-checking every status code with the contract and your permission matrix. A criterion that says `403` where your matrix says `404` (drafts!) is a design decision you must make consciously, not accept by default.

deliverables.text: `spec/requirements.md` with problem statement, personas + permission matrix, FRs, measurable NFRs, threats, out of scope and estimates.
8–10 GitHub Issues created from the *User story* template, each with a refusal criterion.
A merged PR and an `AI_LOG.md` entry (what the assistant invented that you removed).

quiz.q: Which requirement is testable?
options: "An access token expires 900 seconds after it is issued."
quiz.explanation: It has a number a test can check with an injected clock. The others need a measurable threshold first.

quiz.q: A logged-in READER requests someone else's draft by its slug. What should the API answer?
quiz.explanation: `403` would confirm that a post with that slug exists. For resources the caller should not even know about, `404` leaks nothing.

quiz.q: Why is "registration ignores a `role` field" a security requirement?
options: Otherwise a client could register itself as ADMIN (mass assignment)
Roles are stored in another table
quiz.explanation: Mass assignment (OWASP API3: Broken Object Property Level Authorization) happens when a server copies client fields straight into a model. Every new account is a READER; only an ADMIN can change roles.

quiz.q: Which of these is out of scope for v1 according to the brief?
quiz.explanation: It needs an e-mail provider and adds a whole token flow. Writing it down as out of scope protects the schedule.

phases.title: Design (architecture, auth, DB schema, API contract)
phases.heading: Phase 2 · Design: architecture, auth, database schema, API contract
phases.why_md:
Design is where you make the expensive decisions on purpose: how users prove who they are, how a
session survives a stolen token, how the feed pages through thousands of posts without skipping any,
what happens when two people edit the same post, and what an AI is allowed to decide. Writing them down
as diagrams and **Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)** lets a reviewer follow your reasoning in
minutes. The SQL schema is the one artefact that is shared by all three tracks, so a mistake here costs
three times, and a missing constraint is a security bug waiting to happen.
objectives: Draw context, container and sequence diagrams (login + refresh, comment + moderation) in Mermaid.
Write five ADRs: auth design, keyset pagination, optimistic locking, AI moderation with a human in the loop, and why the Java track does not use the Spring Security filter chain.
Design the PostgreSQL schema and write it as migration `spec/db/migrations/V1__init.sql`.
Read the given OpenAPI contract and map each endpoint to a requirement.
Watch your track's migrator apply V1 on start-up.

steps.title: Diagrams in `spec/architecture.md`
steps.content_md:
Mermaid is text, so it diffs and reviews like code. Start with a container diagram:
```text
flowchart TB
    client([HTTP clients: web, mobile, curl]) --> app["DevBlog app :8080"]
    app -- "SQL (source of truth)" --> pg[("PostgreSQL 16")]
    app -. "optional, timeout + fallback" .-> llm[("LLM endpoint")]
```
Wrap it in a code fence with the language `mermaid` and preview it on GitHub or in VS Code (extension
"Markdown Preview Mermaid Support"). Then draw two sequences:
1. **Login → authenticated request → refresh (rotation) → reuse of the old refresh token.**
2. **POST a comment** with the LLM answering, with the LLM down (rules fallback), and an admin approving
   a held comment.

steps.title: ADRs
steps.content_md:
Copy `spec/adr/0000-template.md` five times:
1. `0001-auth-jwt-and-rotating-refresh-tokens.md`: sessions vs JWT-only vs short JWT + opaque rotating
   refresh token. Where is each token stored, how long does it live, how do you log someone out?
2. `0002-keyset-pagination.md`: `OFFSET` vs keyset (`WHERE (published_at, id) < (…)`). What breaks when a
   post is published while someone is on page 2? Why millisecond timestamps in the cursor?
3. `0003-optimistic-locking.md`: last-write-wins vs a `version` column vs `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`.
4. `0004-ai-moderation-human-in-the-loop.md`: what may the AI decide, what happens when it is down or
   returns nonsense, how do you defend against prompt injection inside a comment?
5. `0005-no-spring-security-filter-chain.md` (all tracks read it; it explains a Java choice): use only
   `spring-security-crypto` and write the authorisation checks in the service layer.

Each ADR is one page: context, options with pros/cons, decision, consequences.

steps.title: Schema → `spec/db/migrations/V1__init.sql`
steps.content_md:
Requirements to satisfy:
- `users`: unique, lower-case `email` (enforce lower case with a `CHECK`), `password_hash` (never the
  password), `display_name`, `role` restricted by a `CHECK` to READER/AUTHOR/ADMIN.
- `refresh_tokens`: `token_hash CHAR(64)` (SHA-256 hex, unique), `user_id` with `ON DELETE CASCADE`,
  `expires_at`, nullable `revoked_at`.
- `posts`: unique `slug`, `status` draft/published, `version` for optimistic locking, `published_at`
  (required when published: a `CHECK`), `deleted_at` (soft delete), body ≤ 50 000 chars, and a
  **generated** `tsvector` column for full-text search with a GIN index.
- A **partial index** that matches the feed query exactly:
  `(published_at DESC, id DESC) WHERE status = 'published' AND deleted_at IS NULL`.
- `tags` + `post_tags` (many-to-many, cascade on post delete).
- `comments`: status visible/held/rejected, the AI verdict (label, confidence, provider, fallback,
  reason), `moderated_by`/`moderated_at` for the human decision, `parent_id` for replies.

Name every constraint (`uq_users_email`, `uq_posts_slug`, …) so error handling and tests can refer to
it. Never edit a migration after it is merged. Add `V2__…` instead (you will do that in Phase 7).

ai_prompts.prompt:

quiz.q: Why is the refresh token stored as a SHA-256 hash instead of in plain text?
options: A leaked database dump must not contain usable tokens
So that it can be decoded later
quiz.explanation: Like passwords, tokens are secrets. Because a refresh token has 256 bits of randomness, a fast hash is enough (no bcrypt needed): nobody can brute-force 2²⁵⁶ values.

quiz.q: Why does keyset pagination beat `OFFSET` for the feed?
options: It returns more rows per page
New posts published while you scroll do not shift the pages, and deep pages stay fast
quiz.explanation: `OFFSET 20` after two new posts shows two posts again; keyset (`(published_at, id) < cursor`) continues exactly after the last row you saw, using the index.

quiz.q: Why does the cursor contain the post `id` as well as `published_at`?
options: Two posts can share the same timestamp; the id breaks ties so no post is skipped or repeated
The id is needed for authorisation
PostgreSQL requires two columns in an index
quiz.explanation: Ordering by `(published_at DESC, id DESC)` is total. With the timestamp alone, posts published in the same millisecond could fall between two pages.

quiz.q: Two authors open the same post (version 3). Alice saves first. What happens when Bob saves?
options: The database locks the row until Bob gives up
Bob gets `409 version-conflict` with the current version, reloads and merges
quiz.explanation: `UPDATE … WHERE id = ? AND version = 3` matches nothing after Alice's save made it 4. No locks are held while people type.

quiz.q: In ADR-0004, what is the AI allowed to do with a comment?
options: Delete it if it is confident
Hold it for a human; only an admin can reject it
quiz.explanation: False positives are inevitable. Holding is reversible, so a model mistake costs a delay, not a lost comment. The admin's decision is recorded next to the AI verdict.

quiz.q: What does a partial index `… WHERE status = 'published' AND deleted_at IS NULL` give the feed?
options: It hides drafts from the API automatically
A smaller index that contains exactly the rows the feed query reads, in feed order
It enforces that drafts have no `published_at`
quiz.explanation: The planner can read the first N entries of the index and stop. Drafts and deleted posts never bloat it. The query's `WHERE` must match the index predicate for it to be used.

Bounding what an AI may decide, and designing the fallback before the feature.
Schema design with named constraints, CHECKs, generated columns, partial and GIN indexes, soft delete.

phases.heading: Phase 3 · Implementation in five milestones
phases.why_md:
This is where most tutorials hand you finished code. Here you get the **tests first** instead: the
complete unit suite is already written and switched off. Each milestone turns on a slice of it, you
watch it fail, then you write the smallest code that makes it pass. For security code this matters even
more: an assistant can produce a login that *looks* right and accepts forged tokens. The tests, not
the assistant and not your intuition, decide whether the code is right.
objectives: Implement DevBlog's business logic in your track, one milestone at a time: **M1** validation + text helpers · **M2** auth (bcrypt, JWT, rotating refresh tokens, roles) · **M3** posts (drafts, ownership, optimistic locking, soft delete) · **M4** feed, tags and full-text search · **M5** comments, AI moderation and summaries with offline fallbacks.
Use the pending list to work test-first.
Keep the HTTP layer thin and the business logic (including authorisation) in framework-free services.
Review AI-generated security code critically and catch a planted bug with a test.

steps.title: M1: validation and text helpers (FR-1, FR-6, FR-10)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **validation** and **text**. Every rule has an exact error message in the tests, identical in
all three tracks, because clients and the smoke test depend on them. Watch for the traps the tests
check: e-mails are trimmed and lower-cased; passwords are limited to **72 bytes** (bcrypt silently
ignores the rest), not 72 characters; `version` must be an integer and **booleans are not integers**
(in Python `True` is an `int`; in JavaScript `typeof` helps); `limit` must be ASCII digits only.

Text helpers: `slugify("Hello, World!") == "hello-world"` (NFKD-normalise, drop accents, at most 80
chars, `post` if nothing is left); `excerpt` strips Markdown markers and cuts to 160 chars with `...`;
the feed cursor is base64url **without padding** of `2026-10-02T04:00:00.000Z|42` (ADR-0002).

steps.title: M2: authentication and roles (FR-1 … FR-5, NFR-1, NFR-2)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **security**, **auth** and **api-auth**. Build it in this order:
1. `PasswordHasher`: bcrypt with the configured cost (tests use 4 so they stay fast). `verify` must
   return `false`, not throw, on a malformed hash.
2. `TokenService`: issue an HS256 JWT (`sub`, `role`, `iss`, `iat`, `exp = now + 900 s` from the
   injected clock) and verify it with the **algorithm pinned**. Refresh tokens are 32 random bytes from a
   CSPRNG; only their SHA-256 hex digest is stored.
3. `AuthService`: register (always READER), login (same `401` for unknown e-mail and wrong password,
   with a dummy bcrypt verify for unknown e-mails so the timing matches), refresh with **rotation and
   reuse detection**, logout, `me`, role changes, `authenticate`/`optional` for the `Authorization` header.

<!-- track:java -->

steps.title: M3: posts (FR-6 … FR-9)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **posts** and **api-posts**. Rules the tests check:
- Only AUTHOR/ADMIN create (`403` for READERs). New posts are drafts unless `status: published`.
- Slugs come from the title; on a duplicate-key error retry with `-2`, `-3`, … (insert and catch, never
  "check then insert": two requests can race).
- `get`: a missing post **or** a draft you may not see is `404`, never `403`.
- `update` checks in a fixed order (the tests prove it): payload is an object → `version` present →
  something to update → post exists → you may edit it → fields valid → save with
  `WHERE version = ?` (`409 version-conflict` when nothing was updated). The first publish sets
  `publishedAt`; the slug never changes.
- `delete` is a soft delete (`deleted_at`): user content is never hard-deleted.

Promote Meera with the admin token and write a post:
```bash
ADMIN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"admin@devblog.local","password":"admin-password-123"}' | sed -E 's/.*"accessToken":"([^"]+)".*/\1/')
curl -s -X PATCH localhost:8080/api/v1/admin/users/2/role -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"role":"AUTHOR"}'
# log in as Meera again (her old access token still says READER for up to 15 minutes), then:
curl -si -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/posts -H "Authorization: Bearer $MEERA" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"title":"Docker for beginners","body":"Containers package an app with its dependencies.","tags":["docker"]}'
```

steps.title: M4: feed, tags and search (FR-10, FR-11)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **feed**. The service validates `limit`/`cursor`/`tag`/`q`, asks the repository for
`limit + 1` rows and builds `nextCursor` from the **last row shown** if there was an extra row. The
repository query (ADR-0002):
```sql
SELECT ... FROM posts p JOIN users u ON u.id = p.author_id
WHERE p.status = 'published' AND p.deleted_at IS NULL
  AND (p.published_at, p.id) < ($cursorTs, $cursorId)           -- only with a cursor
  AND p.search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $q)     -- only with q
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM post_tags pt JOIN tags t ON t.id = pt.tag_id
              WHERE pt.post_id = p.id AND t.name = $tag)         -- only with tag
ORDER BY p.published_at DESC, p.id DESC
LIMIT $limitPlusOne;
```
Build the SQL with placeholders for every value; never concatenate `q` or `tag` into the string.
Search with `curl -s 'localhost:8080/api/v1/posts?q=container'`: stemming finds "Containers".

steps.title: M5: comments, AI moderation and summaries (FR-12 … FR-14, NFR-4)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **moderation**, **summaries**, **comments** and **api-comments**. Pieces:
1. `RuleModerator` (offline, deterministic, identical in all tracks): toxic terms as **whole words** →
   `toxic 0.9`; spam phrases → `spam 0.9`; two or more links → `spam 0.75`; otherwise `ok 0.6`.
2. `LlmModerator`: one `POST {LLM_BASE_URL}/chat/completions` (the OpenAI-compatible format that
   Ollama, Gemini and Groq all accept) with the comment inside `<comment>` tags, and a **strict** parser
   for the answer. Anything unexpected throws.
3. `ModerationService`: LLM if configured; on **any** error, the rules with `fallback: true`.
   `held` when the label is not `ok` and the confidence is ≥ 0.7, otherwise `visible`.
4. Summaries: the template takes the first two sentences (≤ 280 chars); the LLM version caps its input
   at 4 000 characters (cost) and falls back to the template on any failure.
5. `CommentService`: comment only on **published** posts; replies only to visible top-level comments
   of the same post; the admin queue and decisions (`approve` → visible, `reject` → rejected, recording
   who and when, keeping the AI verdict).

Run it three ways:
```bash
make run                                                        # rules + template (default, offline)
AI_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9/v1 make run      # unreachable → fallback: true
# Optional, local and free:  docker compose --profile ollama up -d
#   docker compose exec ollama ollama pull llama3.2:1b
#   AI_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1 make run
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/posts/docker-for-beginners/comments -H "Authorization: Bearer $MEERA" \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"body":"click here for free money"}'     # "status":"held"
```
A free Gemini or Groq key also works (`LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_API_KEY` in `.env.example`).
Keep the key in your shell or `.env`, never in Git, and never send real users' comments to a hosted
model without telling them.

steps.title: Review the AI's code (exercise)
steps.content_md:
An assistant produced this `refresh` (pseudo-code). Find the bugs **before** reading on, then point to
the test that catches them.
```text
stored = repo.findRefreshToken(sha256(token))
if stored is None or stored.expiresAt <= now: raise 401
repo.revokeRefreshToken(stored.id, now)
return issue(repo.findUser(stored.userId))
```
It never looks at `revokedAt` and ignores the result of the revoke. An attacker who copied a refresh
token can use it again after the real user has rotated it, and nothing notices; two concurrent requests
with the same token both get fresh sessions. The unit test *"reusing a refresh token revokes every
session"* fails against it (and in Phase 4 the integration test *"concurrent refreshes with one token
let exactly one win"*). Note in `AI_LOG.md` how you found it.

quiz.q: Why must the services use an injected clock?
options: It is faster than the system clock
Tests can move time forward to check token and refresh-token expiry without sleeping
quiz.explanation: `clock.advance(minutes=16)` makes "expired access token" deterministic. Code that calls `now()` directly can only be tested by waiting 15 minutes.

quiz.q: Why is the JWT algorithm pinned to HS256 when verifying?
options: Otherwise a token could choose its own algorithm, e.g. `alg: none`, and skip the signature check
The JWT standard forbids other algorithms
quiz.explanation: Algorithm confusion is a classic JWT vulnerability. The server, not the token, decides how tokens are verified.

quiz.q: Login with an unknown e-mail returns the same `401` as a wrong password. Why also run a dummy bcrypt check?
options: Without it, unknown e-mails answer much faster, which reveals which e-mails have accounts
quiz.explanation: Identical messages are not enough if the timing differs by 50–100 ms. The dummy verify makes both paths cost one bcrypt check.

quiz.q: A refresh token that was already rotated is presented again. What does DevBlog do?
options: Accepts it once more, then revokes it
Revokes all of that user's refresh tokens and returns `401 invalid-refresh-token`
Ignores it and returns the same pair as before
quiz.explanation: A used token coming back means someone has a copy. We cannot tell the thief from the user, so every session ends and the real user logs in again (ADR-0001).

quiz.q: Why do slugs use "insert, catch the duplicate, retry with -2" instead of checking first?
options: Checking is not possible in SQL
Check-then-insert races; the unique constraint is the only reliable judge
The tests require exactly two database calls
quiz.explanation: Two authors publishing "Hello World" at the same moment would both see the slug as free. The database constraint decides.

quiz.q: What must `POST …/comments` do when the LLM endpoint is unreachable?
options: Store the comment as `held` until the LLM is back
Moderate with the rules, store the result with `provider: "rules"` and `fallback: true`, and answer `201`
Return `503` until the LLM is back
quiz.explanation: The AI is an optional layer on a deterministic baseline (NFR-4). Users can always comment, and `fallback` makes the degradation visible.

quiz.q: In the AI-generated `refresh`, what is the bug?
options: It hashes the token before the lookup
It ignores `revokedAt` and the result of the revoke, so a replayed or concurrently used token gets a new session
It re-reads the user from the database
quiz.explanation: Rotation without reuse detection only looks secure. The compare-and-set result is the signal that a token was used twice.

phases.title: Testing (unit, integration, security, coverage)
phases.heading: Phase 4 · Testing: integration, security and concurrency tests, coverage gate
phases.why_md:
Unit tests with in-memory fakes prove your logic. They cannot prove that your SQL is valid, that the
unique e-mail constraint really fires, that the database never sees a password in clear text, or that
two refreshes racing with the same token really let only one through. Integration tests against a
**real** PostgreSQL do. A coverage gate then stops the suite from quietly rotting. Together they let you
change code (or accept an AI's refactor) without fear, which is exactly what you need before CI in Phase 5.
objectives: Explain the test pyramid for DevBlog: unit (fast, many), integration (real database), smoke (black-box, few).
Run the integration suite against the Compose database using a **separate** test database.
Prove security and concurrency behaviour at the database level: hashed secrets, unique constraints, compare-and-set token revocation, optimistic locking in SQL, soft delete.
Enforce ≥ 85 % line coverage locally and understand what the number does and does not mean.

steps.title: Read the security and concurrency tests
steps.content_md:
Open the integration file and find these cases. Each maps to a requirement:
- **passwords and refresh tokens are never stored in clear** (NFR-1, NFR-2): the test reads the rows
  with SQL and checks for a bcrypt prefix and a 64-character hex digest.
- **unique e-mail enforced by the database** (FR-1): even a direct insert of a duplicate fails.
- **concurrent refreshes with one token let exactly one win** (FR-3): several requests race with the
  same refresh token; exactly one gets `200`, and the rest trigger reuse detection.
- **version conflict detected by the update statement** (FR-8) and **soft delete keeps the row** (FR-9).
- **full-text search uses English stemming** and **keyset pagination over the real index** with 25 posts
  sharing one timestamp (FR-10, ADR-0002).
- **health reports DOWN when the database is unreachable** (FR-15) and **migrations recorded**.
- **the admin is bootstrapped from the environment** (FR-5).

quiz.q: Which bug can ONLY an integration test catch here?
options: A wrong error message for a too-long title
A typo in the `UPDATE posts … WHERE version = ?` statement
quiz.explanation: Unit tests use the in-memory repositories, so the SQL never runs there. The other bugs live in pure logic and are covered by unit tests.

quiz.q: How does the integration suite prove that passwords are not stored in clear text?
options: It reads `users.password_hash` with SQL and checks it is a bcrypt hash, not the password
It logs in with the password
It checks the HTTP response does not contain the password
quiz.explanation: The response and the database are different places a secret can leak. Only a test that looks at the stored row proves the storage requirement.

quiz.q: Why does the concurrency test need real parallel requests?
options: The bug only appears when two requests read the same unrevoked token before either writes
To test the connection pool size

The integration tests are not needed

phases.title: CI with GitHub Actions
phases.heading: Phase 5 · Continuous integration with GitHub Actions
phases.why_md:
"It passed on my machine" is not evidence. CI runs the same checks on a clean machine for every push
and pull request, so a broken change never reaches `main`. It is also the cheapest code reviewer you
will ever have. In this phase you grow the starter workflow into a real pipeline: path filters, a
reusable workflow, service containers for integration tests, caching, a coverage artefact and one
required status check.

Every keyword used here is explained slowly in **[docs/github-actions-explained.md](github-actions-explained.md)**.
Read it side by side with the YAML.
objectives: Explain triggers, jobs, steps, runners, `needs`, `if`, matrices, caching and artefacts.
Write a **reusable workflow** (`workflow_call`) that runs one track's full check, and call it three times.
Run integration tests in CI with a PostgreSQL **service container**.
Skip unaffected tracks with a **path filter**, and still have a single required check (`ci-ok`).
Validate the OpenAPI contract in CI and enable **Dependabot**.
Protect `main` so a PR cannot be merged while CI is red.

steps.title: Read the starter workflow
steps.content_md:
Open `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. It is a **matrix** over `[java, python, typescript]`; each matrix job
sets up one toolchain (`if: matrix.track == 'java'`), then runs `make install`, `make lint` and `make test`.
The same Makefile targets exist in every track, so CI does not need three different scripts.

steps.title: Create the reusable workflow
steps.content_md:
Create `.github/workflows/reusable-track-ci.yml` with `on: workflow_call` and an input `track`. Give its job:
- `services:` `postgres:16-alpine` with a health check and a published port,
- `env:` `TEST_DATABASE_URL` pointing at `localhost`,
- the setup steps from the starter, then `make install lint test`,
- a step that creates `devblog_test` (`docker exec ${{ job.services.postgres.id }} psql …`),
- `make coverage` (unit + integration + the 85 % gate),
- `actions/upload-artifact@v4` for the coverage report (`if: always()`).

steps.title: Rewrite `ci.yml` as an orchestrator
steps.content_md:
1. A `changes` job with `dorny/paths-filter@v3` that outputs `docs`, `shared`, `java`, `python`, `typescript`.
2. A `contract` job (only when shared files or docs change): `pipx run openapi-spec-validator spec/openapi.yaml`,
   `shellcheck` on `scripts/*.sh` and `python3 scripts/build-cms.py --check` (the course export must match `docs/`).
3. Three jobs `java`, `python`, `typescript`, each `uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable-track-ci.yml`
   with `if:` on its path output.
4. A final `ci-ok` job with `if: always()` and `needs:` on all of them that fails when any result is
   `failure` or `cancelled`. Skipped is fine.

The reference is at `git show phase-5-end:.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

steps.title: Lint your workflows before pushing
steps.content_md:
```bash
# https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint  (Go binary; also available via Homebrew / Docker)
go install github.com/rhysd/actionlint/cmd/actionlint@latest
actionlint                       # run from the repo root
```
`actionlint` catches typos in expressions, unknown inputs, bad `needs` and shell bugs (via shellcheck)
before GitHub ever sees them.

steps.title: Dependabot
steps.content_md:
Add `.github/dependabot.yml` with one entry per ecosystem: `maven` in `/tracks/java`, `pip` in
`/tracks/python`, `npm` in `/tracks/typescript`, and `github-actions` in `/`. Group minor + patch updates
so you get one PR per ecosystem per week.

steps.title: Protect `main`
steps.content_md:
In your fork: **Settings → Branches → Add branch ruleset** (or classic rule) for `main`:
- Require a pull request before merging.
- Require status checks to pass → add **`ci-ok`** (it appears after the first run).
- Block force pushes.

Because skipped jobs count as success, a docs-only PR still gets a green `ci-ok` quickly.

steps.title: Prove it works
steps.content_md:
Open a PR that breaks one test in **one** track: only that track's job runs (path filter) and `ci-ok`
goes red, so the merge button is blocked. Fix it and watch it go green. Then open a PR that only touches
`spec/openapi.yaml`: all jobs run, because a contract change affects every track.

<paste YAML>

quiz.q: What does `on: workflow_call` mean?
options: The workflow runs when someone calls the repository's API
The workflow can be used as a reusable workflow by other workflows (`jobs.<id>.uses`)
The workflow runs on every push
The workflow can only be run manually
quiz.explanation: A reusable workflow is like a function: it declares `inputs`, and the caller passes them with `with:`.

quiz.q: Why is `ci-ok` the only required check instead of every job?
options: GitHub allows only one required check
With path filters some jobs are skipped; one aggregator job gives a stable name that is green when nothing failed
Reusable workflows cannot be required checks
quiz.explanation: Required checks are matched by name. An aggregator with `if: always()` survives jobs being skipped or renamed.

quiz.q: How do integration tests reach PostgreSQL in CI?
options: They connect to a free cloud database
A `services:` container runs next to the job and its port is published on `localhost`
Docker Compose is started inside the test
quiz.explanation: Service containers live for one job, are health-checked before steps start, and are thrown away afterwards.

quiz.q: What does `cache: npm` (or `maven`/`pip`) in a setup action do?
options: Restores the package download cache keyed by a hash of the lock file, so installs are faster
quiz.explanation: The key changes when `package-lock.json` / `pom.xml` / `requirements-dev.txt` changes, so you never get stale dependencies.

quiz.q: Which default `permissions` block is safest for a CI workflow that only reads code?
quiz.explanation: Least privilege. Jobs that need more (e.g. pushing images) ask for it explicitly, as `deploy.yml` does in Phase 6.

recap: Workflow anatomy: triggers, jobs, steps, runners, `needs`, `if`, `defaults`, `concurrency`.
Reusable workflows with inputs, and an orchestrator workflow that calls them.
Service containers for real integration tests in CI.
Path filters plus an aggregator job for fast and safe required checks.
Caching, artefacts, actionlint, Dependabot and branch protection.

phases.title: Containerise, deliver, and (optionally) deploy to a free tier
phases.heading: Phase 6 · Containerise, deliver and (optionally) deploy
phases.why_md:
A container image is the unit you actually ship: the same bytes run on your laptop, in CI and in
the cloud. In this phase you write a production-grade Dockerfile, run the whole stack with one
command, prove it with a black-box smoke test, and publish versioned images to GitHub Container
Registry (GHCR) automatically on every release tag. Deploying to the cloud is **optional**: everything
graded in this phase works offline on your laptop.
objectives: Write a multi-stage, non-root Dockerfile with a `HEALTHCHECK` for your track.
Add your app to `docker-compose.yml` as a profile and start the stack with `docker compose --profile <track> up`.
Run the language-agnostic smoke test against your container (and against the other tracks' images).
Add a Docker build + smoke job to CI.
Write `deploy.yml`: on a `v*.*.*` tag, build and push images to GHCR; optionally trigger a Render deploy that is **skipped gracefully** when no secret is configured.
Cut release **v1.0.0** with a CHANGELOG entry.

steps.title: The Dockerfile (build context = repository root)
steps.content_md:
All tracks copy the shared migrations into the image, so the build context is the repo root and the
Dockerfile lives in the track: `docker build -f tracks/<track>/Dockerfile .`. Rules:
- **Multi-stage:** compilers and dev dependencies stay in the build stage.
- **Dependencies before source:** copy the manifest, install, then copy `src`, so code changes reuse the dependency layer.
- **Non-root user**, `EXPOSE 8080`, `HEALTHCHECK` hitting `/health`, `MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations`.

<!-- track:java -->
```dockerfile
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/java/pom.xml tracks/java/checkstyle.xml ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q dependency:go-offline
COPY tracks/java/src ./src
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q package -DskipTests -Dcheckstyle.skip -Djacoco.skip=true \
    && java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/app.jar extract --layers --launcher --destination /extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
ENV PORT=8080 MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75"
WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 app
COPY --from=build /extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/application/ ./
COPY spec/db/migrations ./migrations
USER 10001
HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health > /dev/null || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
```
(abridged; the full file installs `curl` and sets the health-check timings)
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/python/requirements.txt .
RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PORT=8080 MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels && useradd --system --uid 10001 appuser
COPY tracks/python/app ./app
COPY spec/db/migrations ./migrations
USER 10001
HEALTHCHECK CMD python -c "import urllib.request,sys; sys.exit(0 if urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8080/health', timeout=2).status == 200 else 1)"
CMD ["python", "-m", "app"]
```
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/typescript/package.json tracks/typescript/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --no-audit --no-fund
COPY tracks/typescript/tsconfig.json tracks/typescript/tsconfig.build.json ./
COPY tracks/typescript/src ./src
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=8080 MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations
WORKDIR /app
COPY tracks/typescript/package.json tracks/typescript/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev --no-audit --no-fund && npm cache clean --force
COPY --from=build /build/dist ./dist
COPY spec/db/migrations ./migrations
USER node
HEALTHCHECK CMD node -e "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8080/health').then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1)).catch(()=>process.exit(1))"
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
```
<!-- /track -->

The root `.dockerignore` (already in the starter: `**/node_modules`, `**/.venv`, `**/target`, `.git`, …)
keeps the build context small and excludes `.env`, so local secrets never reach the Docker daemon. Build and check the size and user:

```bash
docker image ls devblog-<track>
docker run --rm --entrypoint id devblog-<track>:local      # must NOT be uid=0
```

- **Multi-stage:** compilers and dev dependencies stay in the build stage.
- **Dependencies before source:** copy the manifest, install, then copy `src`, so code changes reuse the dependency layer.
- **Non-root user**, `EXPOSE 8080`, `HEALTHCHECK` hitting `/health`, `MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations`.

```dockerfile
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/java/pom.xml tracks/java/checkstyle.xml ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q dependency:go-offline
COPY tracks/java/src ./src
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q package -DskipTests -Dcheckstyle.skip -Djacoco.skip=true \
    && java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/app.jar extract --layers --launcher --destination /extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
ENV PORT=8080 MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75"
WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 app
COPY --from=build /extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/application/ ./
COPY spec/db/migrations ./migrations
USER 10001
HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health > /dev/null || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
```

```bash
docker run --rm --entrypoint id devblog-<track>:local      # must NOT be uid=0
```

steps.title: Compose profiles: one command for the whole stack
steps.content_md:
Add a service per track to `docker-compose.yml` under a **profile**, sharing one block of environment
variables (a YAML anchor `x-app-env`), `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`, and port
`${APP_PORT:-8080}:8080`. Inside Compose the app reaches the database as `postgres:5432`, not `localhost`.
The Compose file sets **local-only** values for `JWT_SECRET` and the first admin
(`admin@devblog.local` / `admin-password-123`) through `${VAR:-default}`, so `docker compose up` works out
of the box. A real deployment sets its own values: the defaults are public, in this repository.
```bash
docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait
docker compose ps
```

steps.title: Smoke test (the same for every track)
steps.content_md:
```bash
scripts/smoke-test.sh                      # default http://localhost:8080
```
It checks 53 behaviours with only `bash` + `curl`: health, registration (the `role` field is
ignored), duplicate e-mail, `problem+json` errors, login, `/me` with and without a token, refresh
rotation and **reuse detection** (the whole token family is revoked), then (logged in as the Compose
admin) role promotion, `403` for READERs, drafts that are `404` for others, publishing, optimistic
locking (`409`), tag feed, full-text search, summaries, comments, a spammy comment that is **held** and
hidden, the admin queue and a decision, and soft delete. It creates its own uniquely named users and
posts, so it is safe to run repeatedly.
Against a deployment, pass the admin credentials as `SMOKE_ADMIN_EMAIL` / `SMOKE_ADMIN_PASSWORD`. If you
cannot, `SMOKE_ALLOW_NO_ADMIN=true` turns the admin-dependent block into one `SKIP` instead of failures.
Because the contract is shared, try another track's
image against the same database: `docker compose stop app-<yours>` and `docker compose --profile python up -d`.
Same results. Also run the AI fallback check:
```bash
AI_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9/v1 LLM_TIMEOUT_MS=1000 docker compose --profile <track> up -d --wait
EXPECT_FALLBACK=true scripts/smoke-test.sh      # 55 checks: moderation and summaries report fallback: true
```

steps.title: CI: build the image and smoke-test it
steps.content_md:
Add a `docker` job (matrix over tracks) to `ci.yml`: `docker/setup-buildx-action`,
`docker/build-push-action` with `load: true` and the GitHub Actions layer cache (`cache-from/to: type=gha`),
then `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --no-build --wait`, the smoke test, logs on failure and `down -v`.

steps.title: Continuous delivery to GHCR: `deploy.yml`
steps.content_md:
Trigger on `push: tags: ["v*.*.*"]`. The job needs `permissions: packages: write` and logs in to
`ghcr.io` with the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`; no personal token required. Image names must be lower-case
(the org is `AICanCode-org`), so compute `ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER,,}/devblog-<track>`.
`docker/metadata-action` turns tag `v1.0.0` into image tags `1.0.0`, `1.0`, `sha-<short>` and `latest`.
Read `docs/github-actions-explained.md` §9–§12 for every detail.

steps.title: Release v1.0.0
steps.content_md:
```bash
# update CHANGELOG.md: move "Unreleased" items under "## [1.0.0] - <date>"
git commit -am "chore(release): v1.0.0"
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "DevBlog v1.0.0"
git push origin main --follow-tags
```
Watch **Actions → Deploy**: three images appear under your profile's **Packages**. New GHCR packages
are **private** by default. Make one public (Package settings → Change visibility) if a host should pull
it without credentials.

steps.title: OPTIONAL: deploy to a free tier
steps.content_md:
You do not need a cloud account to finish this course. If you want a public URL:

| Piece | Free option | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| App | **Render** web service from an *existing image* (`ghcr.io/<you>/devblog-<track>:latest`) | Free instances spin down after 15 minutes without traffic; the next request takes about a minute (cold start). |
| PostgreSQL | **Neon** free tier | Use its connection string as `DATABASE_URL` and keep `?sslmode=require`. Java: if the string contains `channel_binding=require`, remove that parameter. Render's own free Postgres also works but **expires after 30 days**. |
| Secrets | Render env vars | Set your own `JWT_SECRET` (`openssl rand -base64 48`), `ADMIN_EMAIL`, a strong `ADMIN_PASSWORD`. Never reuse the Compose defaults. |
| LLM | none (rules/template), or a free Gemini / Groq key | `AI_PROVIDER=llm`, `LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_API_KEY` as Render env vars. Tell your users if comments are sent to a hosted model. |

Free-tier limits change. Check each provider's pricing page before you rely on it. Fly.io is **not**
used: at the time of writing it needs a payment method and bills usage, with no free tier for new accounts.

To let CI deploy for you:
1. Render → your service → **Settings → Deploy Hook**: copy the URL.
2. GitHub → **Settings → Environments → New environment `production`** (optionally add yourself as a
   required reviewer). Add the **secret** `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` and the **variables** `RENDER_APP_URL`
   (e.g. `https://devblog-xyz.onrender.com`) and `DEPLOY_TRACK` (`java`, `python` or `typescript`).
   Optionally add the secrets `SMOKE_ADMIN_EMAIL` / `SMOKE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` so the live smoke test also
   runs the admin steps.
3. Push a tag. The `render` job calls the hook with `imgURL=` set to the exact version, waits for
   `/health`, and runs the smoke test against the live URL. Without the secret the job prints a notice
   and **succeeds**, so forks without cloud accounts stay green.

deliverables.text: `tracks/<track>/Dockerfile` (multi-stage, non-root, HEALTHCHECK).
`docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait` + `scripts/smoke-test.sh`: all checks pass, and `EXPECT_FALLBACK=true` passes with an unreachable LLM.
CI `docker` job green; `deploy.yml` pushed images to GHCR for tag `v1.0.0`.
`CHANGELOG.md` with `[1.0.0]`; `docs/runbook.md` with start/stop/rollback/rotate-secret steps.
Optional: a live URL in your README and a green `render` job.

quiz.q: Why do the Dockerfiles copy the dependency manifest before the source code?
options: So that the dependency layer is cached and only rebuilt when the manifest changes
quiz.explanation: Layers are cached top-down; anything after a changed layer is rebuilt. Source changes often, dependencies rarely.

quiz.q: Inside Docker Compose, which `DATABASE_URL` host does the app use?
quiz.explanation: Each container has its own `localhost`. Compose gives services DNS names on a shared network.

quiz.q: Why does the image push use `${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER,,}`?
options: GHCR image names must be lower-case and the org name `AICanCode-org` has capitals
quiz.explanation: `,,` is bash's lower-case expansion. `ghcr.io/AICanCode-org/...` would be rejected.

quiz.q: A fork has no `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` secret. What does the `render` job do on a tag push?
options: Prints a notice and succeeds; the image is still pushed to the fork's GHCR
Waits for someone to add the secret
quiz.explanation: Optional infrastructure must not make the pipeline red. Secrets are read into `env:` and tested with `if: env.X == ''`.

quiz.q: Why are free hosting instances slow on the first request after a while?
options: Idle instances are stopped to save cost and must boot again (cold start)
quiz.explanation: That is why the deploy job polls `/health` for up to 10 minutes before smoke-testing.

quiz.q: Why must a deployment never use the `JWT_SECRET` from `docker-compose.yml`?
options: It is public in the repository, so anyone could sign a valid ADMIN token for your API
quiz.explanation: Whoever knows an HS256 secret can mint any token. Defaults are for laptops; deployments get their own secret from the host's environment variables.

recap: Production Dockerfiles: multi-stage, layer caching, non-root, health checks, `.dockerignore`.
Compose profiles to run any track against the same dependencies with one command.
Black-box smoke tests that work for any implementation of a contract.
Image builds with layer caching in CI, and delivery to GHCR with the built-in token on version tags.
Optional, secret-gated deployment that degrades gracefully, plus free-tier trade-offs (cold starts, TLS URLs).
Semantic versioning and a CHANGELOG-driven release.

phases.title: Observability and maintenance
phases.heading: Phase 7 · Observability and maintenance (v1.1.0)
phases.why_md:
Shipping v1.0.0 is the start, not the end. In production you have to answer "is it working right now,
and if not, why?" without attaching a debugger. That needs three things: **logs** you can search,
**metrics** you can graph, and a **request ID** that ties a reader's complaint to log lines. DevBlog
also depends on something you do not control, an LLM, so you will run a **game day** where the LLM
hangs, measure what readers feel, and fix it with a **circuit breaker**. Finally you make your
first **maintenance change**, a schema migration plus a backward-compatible API field, and release it
safely as v1.1.0.
objectives: Give every request an `X-Request-ID` (reuse a safe incoming one, or generate a UUID) and put it in every log line.
Emit structured **JSON logs**: one object per line, one access-log line per request.
Expose `/metrics` in Prometheus text format with seven counters that are identical in every track.
Run a **game day**: make the LLM hang, measure comment latency, write a short blameless post-mortem.
Add an LLM **circuit breaker** (3 failures in a row → open for 30 s → one half-open trial).
Ship a backward-compatible change: `V2__post_cover_image.sql` + `coverImageUrl` in the API, OpenAPI 1.1.0, CHANGELOG, tag `v1.1.0`.
Review and merge one Dependabot PR.

steps.title: Request IDs
steps.content_md:
Rule (shared by all tracks): if the incoming `X-Request-ID` matches `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$`, echo it;
otherwise generate a UUID. Never echo arbitrary input: a header containing a newline could inject
fake log lines or headers.

<!-- track:java -->
A `OncePerRequestFilter` (`web/RequestIdFilter.java`) sets the response header, puts `requestId` in
the SLF4J **MDC** (so every log line in that request carries it) and logs one `devblog.access` line
with `method`, `path`, `status` and `durationMs` using the fluent API
`LOG.atInfo().addKeyValue("status", …).log()`. `@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)` makes it the first
filter, so even a `401` or a `404` gets an ID (there is no Spring Security filter chain, see ADR-0005).
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
A Starlette middleware (`app/observability.py`) stores the ID in `request.state`, sets the response
header and logs one `devblog.access` record with `extra={"fields": {...}}`. The middleware wraps the
whole app, so error responses (`400`, `401`, `404`) carry the header too.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
Fastify has request IDs built in: `genReqId` (calling `incomingOrNewId()` from `src/observability.ts`)
with `requestIdHeader: false`, so we validate the incoming value ourselves, and a `LogController` with `requestIdLogLabel: "requestId"`.
An `onSend` hook copies `request.id` into the `X-Request-ID` response header.
<!-- /track -->

steps.title: `/metrics`
steps.content_md:
Seven counters, same names in all tracks (see `GET /metrics` in `spec/openapi.yaml`):

| Counter | Incremented when |
|---|---|
| `devblog_users_registered_total` | a registration succeeds |
| `devblog_logins_failed_total` | a login is rejected (watch it for credential stuffing) |
| `devblog_posts_published_total` | a post becomes `published` |
| `devblog_comments_created_total` | a comment is stored |
| `devblog_comments_held_total` | moderation holds a comment for review |
| `devblog_ai_fallback_total` | an AI call fell back to the offline rules/template |
| `devblog_llm_short_circuits_total` | the circuit breaker skipped an LLM call (Step 7.5) |

They are hand-rolled on purpose: the Prometheus text format is just
```text
# HELP devblog_logins_failed_total Login attempts answered with 401.
# TYPE devblog_logins_failed_total counter
devblog_logins_failed_total 3
```
In a bigger service you would use Micrometer (Java), `prometheus-client` (Python) or `prom-client` (Node).
`/metrics` is public in this course project; in production you would restrict it to the scraper's network.

steps.title: Game day: the LLM hangs
steps.content_md:
A dead LLM is easy: the connection is refused and the fallback answers in milliseconds. A **hanging** LLM
is worse: it accepts the connection and never answers, so every request that needs it waits for the full
`LLM_TIMEOUT_MS` (5 s by default). That is what an overloaded hosted model or a stuck local Ollama looks like.
1. Start the stack at v1.0.0: `git switch --detach v1.0.0`, `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait`.
2. Get the script from the reference: `git show phase-7-end:scripts/game-day.sh > /tmp/game-day.sh && chmod +x /tmp/game-day.sh`,
   then `/tmp/game-day.sh <track>`. It creates a published post and a reader, then runs four phases of
   10 comments each: **offline** baseline, a **healthy** fake LLM, the fake LLM **hanging**, and the LLM
   **back**. The fake LLM is a 15-line Python HTTP server in a throw-away container on the Compose network
   (`MODE=ok` answers like `/v1/chat/completions`, `MODE=hang` never answers), so no model download and no API key.
3. Write down for each phase: status codes, average and maximum latency, the moderation `provider` and
   `fallback` flag, the warnings in the logs, and (from v1.1) the counters. Is any comment lost? Is any
   comment slow? What would 50 comments a minute feel like?
4. Write `docs/postmortem-<date>-llm-hang.md`: summary, impact, timeline, root cause, what went well,
   what to improve, action items. Blameless: describe systems, not people. Read the reference
   post-mortem **after** writing yours (`git show phase-7-end:docs/postmortem-2026-10-02-llm-hang.md`).

steps.title: Fix: an LLM circuit breaker
steps.content_md:
Wrap the one LLM client (shared by moderation and summaries) in a `CircuitBreaker`:
- **CLOSED:** calls go through. 3 failures **in a row** open the circuit.
- **OPEN:** calls fail immediately (the caller uses its offline fallback) for 30 s, and
  `devblog_llm_short_circuits_total` is incremented.
- **HALF-OPEN:** after the cooldown, exactly **one** trial call goes through. Success closes the circuit;
  failure re-opens it for another 30 s.

Test it with a fake clock and a fake client (no sleeping in tests): 3 failures → the 4th call does not reach
the client; advance the clock 30 s → one trial; a concurrent second call during the trial is short-circuited.

<!-- track:java -->
`ai/CircuitBreaker.java` implements `LlmClient`, so `AppConfig` wraps the HTTP client once and both
`LlmModerator` and `LlmSummarizer` receive the wrapped instance. State changes are `synchronized`;
the slow HTTP call happens **outside** the lock.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
`CircuitBreaker` in `app/ai.py` has the same `chat()` signature as the HTTP client, a `threading.Lock`
around state changes and `time.monotonic` as the default clock (wall-clock time can jump).
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
`CircuitBreaker` in `src/ai.ts` wraps the client's `chat()`. Node is single-threaded, but `await` still
interleaves requests, so the `trialRunning` flag matters exactly as it does in Java and Python.
<!-- /track -->

Re-run the game day on your branch: in the *hang* phase the first 3 comments still wait for the timeout,
the rest answer in milliseconds with `fallback: true`. In the *back* phase the circuit stays open until the
30 s cooldown has passed, then one trial call closes it again.

steps.title: Maintenance change: `coverImageUrl` (v1.1.0)
steps.content_md:
1. `spec/db/migrations/V2__post_cover_image.sql`: `ALTER TABLE posts ADD COLUMN cover_image_url VARCHAR(2048);`
   Nullable, no default, so v1.0.0 code keeps working against the new schema.
2. `CreatePostRequest` / `UpdatePostRequest` accept an **optional** `coverImageUrl`: an absolute `http(s)` URL
   (validated with the regex in the OpenAPI spec; `javascript:` URLs are rejected), `null` clears it.
3. `Post` and `PostListItem` gain `coverImageUrl` (null when not set). Adding a field is backward compatible;
   removing or renaming one is not.
4. `spec/openapi.yaml` → `version: 1.1.0`; `CHANGELOG.md` → `## [1.1.0]`; bump the track's version.
5. Tests first: validation tests for the URL, an API test that sets and clears it, an integration test that
   the column round-trips.
6. Release: `git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "DevBlog v1.1.0" && git push origin main --follow-tags`.
   `deploy.yml` publishes `:1.1.0` and moves `:latest`.

steps.title: Merge a Dependabot PR
steps.content_md:
Pick one grouped update. Read its release notes, check that CI is green **including integration tests**,
run it locally if it is a major version, then merge. Write down in `AI_LOG.md` or the PR what you checked.

ai_prompts.title: Structured logging setup
ai_prompts.prompt:
In <Spring Boot 4 | FastAPI | Fastify 5> I want one JSON log line per request with requestId, method,
path, status and durationMs, where requestId comes from a validated X-Request-ID header or a new UUID
and appears on every log line of that request, including 401 responses from the auth layer. Show the
minimal code with no new dependencies, and explain how the request ID is propagated (MDC / contextvars /
child logger). Passwords and tokens must never be logged.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: sending a request with `X-Request-ID: demo-123` and with a malicious value (`$'bad\nInjected: 1'` in bash). The first must be echoed and logged, the second replaced by a UUID. Check `docker compose logs` shows valid JSON (`| jq .`) and that `grep -i bearer` finds nothing.

ai_prompts.title: Review my circuit breaker
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is my LLM circuit breaker in <language>: <paste>. Rules: 3 consecutive failures open it for 30 s,
then exactly one half-open trial; success closes, failure re-opens. Find race conditions (two requests
during the trial), places where the slow call happens while holding a lock, and missing tests. Suggest
tests that use a fake clock instead of sleeping.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: running the suggested tests and the game day. The short-circuit counter in `/metrics` must grow by one for every comment after the third in the *hang* phase.

ai_prompts.title: Is this migration backward compatible?
ai_prompts.prompt:
I run several app instances and deploy one at a time. Is this migration safe to apply while the old
version is still serving traffic? <paste V2 SQL> What would make it unsafe (NOT NULL, defaults on big
tables, renames)? How would I roll it back?
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: running the **v1.0.0** image against a database that already has V2 applied (`git switch --detach v1.0.0`, `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build`) and running the v1.0.0 smoke test: it must still pass.

deliverables.text: `X-Request-ID` echoed/generated; JSON access logs visible in `docker compose logs`, no tokens in them.
`/metrics` with the seven counters; the v1.1 smoke test passes (57 checks).
`docs/postmortem-…-llm-hang.md` with real numbers from your game day.
Circuit breaker with fake-clock tests; the game day re-run shows fast fallbacks after 3 failures.
`V2__post_cover_image.sql`, `coverImageUrl` in the API, OpenAPI 1.1.0, CHANGELOG, tag `v1.1.0`.
One merged Dependabot PR.

quiz.q: Why validate an incoming `X-Request-ID` before echoing it?
options: An unvalidated value could inject newlines or fake fields into logs and headers
quiz.explanation: Treat every header as untrusted input. A strict allow-list regex is the simplest defence.

quiz.q: During the game day every comment still returned 201. Why is a hanging LLM still an incident?
options: Every comment waited for the full LLM timeout, so writers felt seconds of latency and server threads/connections were tied up
quiz.explanation: Graceful degradation kept correctness (the rules fallback answered) but not latency. Availability is also about how long users wait.

quiz.q: What does the circuit breaker do in the OPEN state?
options: Skips the LLM call immediately so the caller uses its offline fallback, until the cooldown ends
Switches to a different LLM provider
quiz.explanation: It turns a slow failure into a fast one. After the cooldown one half-open trial checks whether the LLM has recovered.

quiz.q: Why is `ADD COLUMN cover_image_url VARCHAR(2048)` (nullable, no default) the safe choice?
options: Postgres does not support `NOT NULL` columns
v1.0.0 code that does not know the column keeps working, and the change is instant
quiz.explanation: Expand first, (optionally) contract later. A `NOT NULL` column would break inserts from v1.0.0 during a rolling deploy.

quiz.q: Adding `coverImageUrl` to the response is a … change.
quiz.explanation: SemVer: new optional fields are minor. Removing or renaming a field would be major (2.0.0).

quiz.q: Which metric would you alert on to spot a credential-stuffing attack?
quiz.explanation: Many rejected logins in a short time is the classic signal. The fix (rate limiting per IP/account) is listed as a gap in Phase 8.

quiz.q: What makes a post-mortem "blameless"?
options: It focuses on how the system and process allowed the failure, not on who made a mistake
quiz.explanation: People hide problems when they fear blame. Blameless reviews produce better action items.

recap: Correlation IDs, MDC/context propagation and structured JSON logs without secrets.
Prometheus counters and the text exposition format.
Game days, blameless post-mortems, and why "hangs" is worse than "down".
The circuit-breaker pattern, tested with a fake clock.
Expand-style, backward-compatible migrations and SemVer minor releases.
Dependency maintenance with Dependabot, and the role of CI as the safety net.
