### Q4. What does `cache: npm` (or `maven`/`pip`) in a setup action do?
- [ ] Caches the build output
- [x] Restores the package download cache keyed by a hash of the lock file, so installs are faster
- [ ] Commits `node_modules` to the repo
- [ ] Skips the install step
> **Answer:** The key changes when `package-lock.json` / `pom.xml` / `requirements-dev.txt` changes, so you never get stale dependencies.

### Q5. Which default `permissions` block is safest for a CI workflow that only reads code?
- [ ] `permissions: write-all`
- [x] `permissions: contents: read`
- [ ] No block at all
- [ ] `permissions: packages: write`
> **Answer:** Least privilege. Jobs that need more (e.g. pushing images) ask for it explicitly, as `deploy.yml` does in Phase 6.

## 7. What you learned
- Workflow anatomy: triggers, jobs, steps, runners, `needs`, `if`, `defaults`, `concurrency`.
- Reusable workflows with inputs, and an orchestrator workflow that calls them.
- Service containers for real integration tests in CI.
- Path filters plus an aggregator job for fast and safe required checks.
- Caching, artefacts, actionlint, Dependabot and branch protection.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-6 phase-5-end
git diff phase-4-end phase-5-end -- .github/
git checkout phase-5-end -- .github/          # take the reference workflows
```

steps.title: Phase 6 · Containerise, deliver and (optionally) deploy
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
A container image is the unit you actually ship: the same bytes run on your laptop, in CI and in
the cloud. In this phase you write a production-grade Dockerfile, run the whole stack with one
command, prove it with a black-box smoke test, and publish versioned images to GitHub Container
Registry (GHCR) automatically on every release tag. Deploying to the cloud is **optional**: everything
graded in this phase works offline on your laptop.

## 2. Objectives
- Write a multi-stage, non-root Dockerfile with a `HEALTHCHECK` for your track.
- Add your app to `docker-compose.yml` as a profile and start the stack with `docker compose --profile <track> up`.
- Run the language-agnostic smoke test against your container (and against the other tracks' images).
- Add a Docker build + smoke job to CI.
- Write `deploy.yml`: on a `v*.*.*` tag, build and push images to GHCR; optionally trigger a Render
  deploy that is **skipped gracefully** when no secret is configured.
- Cut release **v1.0.0** with a CHANGELOG entry.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 6.1 · The Dockerfile (build context = repository root)
All tracks copy the shared migrations into the image, so the build context is the repo root and the
Dockerfile lives in the track: `docker build -f tracks/<track>/Dockerfile .`. Rules:
- **Multi-stage:** compilers and dev dependencies stay in the build stage.
- **Dependencies before source:** copy the manifest, install, then copy `src`, so code changes reuse the dependency layer.
- **Non-root user**, `EXPOSE 8080`, `HEALTHCHECK` hitting `/health`, `MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations`.

<!-- track:java -->
```dockerfile
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/java/pom.xml tracks/java/checkstyle.xml ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q dependency:go-offline
COPY tracks/java/src ./src
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q package -DskipTests -Dcheckstyle.skip -Djacoco.skip=true \
    && java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/app.jar extract --layers --launcher --destination /extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
ENV PORT=8080 MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75"
WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 app
COPY --from=build /extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/application/ ./
COPY spec/db/migrations ./migrations
USER 10001
HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health > /dev/null || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
```
(abridged; the full file installs `curl` and sets the health-check timings)
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/python/requirements.txt .
RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PORT=8080 MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels && useradd --system --uid 10001 appuser
COPY tracks/python/app ./app
COPY spec/db/migrations ./migrations
USER 10001
HEALTHCHECK CMD python -c "import urllib.request,sys; sys.exit(0 if urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8080/health', timeout=2).status == 200 else 1)"
CMD ["python", "-m", "app"]
```
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/typescript/package.json tracks/typescript/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --no-audit --no-fund
COPY tracks/typescript/tsconfig.json tracks/typescript/tsconfig.build.json ./
COPY tracks/typescript/src ./src
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=8080 MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations
WORKDIR /app
COPY tracks/typescript/package.json tracks/typescript/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev --no-audit --no-fund && npm cache clean --force
COPY --from=build /build/dist ./dist
COPY spec/db/migrations ./migrations
USER node
HEALTHCHECK CMD node -e "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8080/health').then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1)).catch(()=>process.exit(1))"
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
```
<!-- /track -->

The root `.dockerignore` (already in the starter: `**/node_modules`, `**/.venv`, `**/target`, `.git`, …)
keeps the build context small and excludes `.env`, so local secrets never reach the Docker daemon. Build and check the size and user:
```bash
docker build -f tracks/<track>/Dockerfile -t devblog-<track>:local .
docker image ls devblog-<track>
docker run --rm --entrypoint id devblog-<track>:local      # must NOT be uid=0
```

### Step 6.2 · Compose profiles: one command for the whole stack
Add a service per track to `docker-compose.yml` under a **profile**, sharing one block of environment
variables (a YAML anchor `x-app-env`), `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`, and port
`${APP_PORT:-8080}:8080`. Inside Compose the app reaches the database as `postgres:5432`, not `localhost`.
The Compose file sets **local-only** values for `JWT_SECRET` and the first admin
(`admin@devblog.local` / `admin-password-123`) through `${VAR:-default}`, so `docker compose up` works out
of the box. A real deployment sets its own values: the defaults are public, in this repository.
```bash
docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait
docker compose ps
```

### Step 6.3 · Smoke test (the same for every track)
```bash
scripts/smoke-test.sh                      # default http://localhost:8080
```
It checks 53 behaviours with only `bash` + `curl`: health, registration (the `role` field is
ignored), duplicate e-mail, `problem+json` errors, login, `/me` with and without a token, refresh
rotation and **reuse detection** (the whole token family is revoked), then (logged in as the Compose
admin) role promotion, `403` for READERs, drafts that are `404` for others, publishing, optimistic
locking (`409`), tag feed, full-text search, summaries, comments, a spammy comment that is **held** and
hidden, the admin queue and a decision, and soft delete. It creates its own uniquely named users and
posts, so it is safe to run repeatedly.
Against a deployment, pass the admin credentials as `SMOKE_ADMIN_EMAIL` / `SMOKE_ADMIN_PASSWORD`. If you
cannot, `SMOKE_ALLOW_NO_ADMIN=true` turns the admin-dependent block into one `SKIP` instead of failures.
Because the contract is shared, try another track's
image against the same database: `docker compose stop app-<yours>` and `docker compose --profile python up -d`.
Same results. Also run the AI fallback check:
```bash
AI_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9/v1 LLM_TIMEOUT_MS=1000 docker compose --profile <track> up -d --wait
EXPECT_FALLBACK=true scripts/smoke-test.sh      # 55 checks: moderation and summaries report fallback: true
```

### Step 6.4 · CI: build the image and smoke-test it
Add a `docker` job (matrix over tracks) to `ci.yml`: `docker/setup-buildx-action`,
`docker/build-push-action` with `load: true` and the GitHub Actions layer cache (`cache-from/to: type=gha`),
then `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --no-build --wait`, the smoke test, logs on failure and `down -v`.

### Step 6.5 · Continuous delivery to GHCR: `deploy.yml`
Trigger on `push: tags: ["v*.*.*"]`. The job needs `permissions: packages: write` and logs in to
`ghcr.io` with the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`; no personal token required. Image names must be lower-case
(the org is `AICanCode-org`), so compute `ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER,,}/devblog-<track>`.
`docker/metadata-action` turns tag `v1.0.0` into image tags `1.0.0`, `1.0`, `sha-<short>` and `latest`.
Read `docs/github-actions-explained.md` §9–§12 for every detail.

### Step 6.6 · Release v1.0.0
```bash
# update CHANGELOG.md: move "Unreleased" items under "## [1.0.0] - <date>"
git commit -am "chore(release): v1.0.0"
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "DevBlog v1.0.0"
git push origin main --follow-tags
```
Watch **Actions → Deploy**: three images appear under your profile's **Packages**. New GHCR packages
are **private** by default. Make one public (Package settings → Change visibility) if a host should pull
it without credentials.

### Step 6.7 · OPTIONAL: deploy to a free tier
You do not need a cloud account to finish this course. If you want a public URL:

| Piece | Free option | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| App | **Render** web service from an *existing image* (`ghcr.io/<you>/devblog-<track>:latest`) | Free instances spin down after 15 minutes without traffic; the next request takes about a minute (cold start). |
| PostgreSQL | **Neon** free tier | Use its connection string as `DATABASE_URL` and keep `?sslmode=require`. Java: if the string contains `channel_binding=require`, remove that parameter. Render's own free Postgres also works but **expires after 30 days**. |
| Secrets | Render env vars | Set your own `JWT_SECRET` (`openssl rand -base64 48`), `ADMIN_EMAIL`, a strong `ADMIN_PASSWORD`. Never reuse the Compose defaults. |
| LLM | none (rules/template), or a free Gemini / Groq key | `AI_PROVIDER=llm`, `LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_API_KEY` as Render env vars. Tell your users if comments are sent to a hosted model. |

Free-tier limits change. Check each provider's pricing page before you rely on it. Fly.io is **not**
used: at the time of writing it needs a payment method and bills usage, with no free tier for new accounts.

To let CI deploy for you:
1. Render → your service → **Settings → Deploy Hook**: copy the URL.
2. GitHub → **Settings → Environments → New environment `production`** (optionally add yourself as a
   required reviewer). Add the **secret** `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` and the **variables** `RENDER_APP_URL`
   (e.g. `https://devblog-xyz.onrender.com`) and `DEPLOY_TRACK` (`java`, `python` or `typescript`).
   Optionally add the secrets `SMOKE_ADMIN_EMAIL` / `SMOKE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` so the live smoke test also
   runs the admin steps.
3. Push a tag. The `render` job calls the hook with `imgURL=` set to the exact version, waits for
   `/health`, and runs the smoke test against the live URL. Without the secret the job prints a notice
   and **succeeds**, so forks without cloud accounts stay green.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Review my Dockerfile
```text
Review this Dockerfile for a <Spring Boot 4 / FastAPI / Fastify> service. Check: multi-stage, layer
caching order, non-root user, HEALTHCHECK, image size, secrets leaking into layers, pinned base image
versions, and anything that would differ between my laptop (amd64/arm64) and CI. <paste Dockerfile>
```
**Verify the output by:** rebuilding and measuring: `docker image ls` (size), `docker run --rm --entrypoint id`
(uid), `docker history` (no secrets, small layers), and `docker compose up --wait` (health check passes).

### Prompt 2: Explain the deploy workflow's security model
```text
In this workflow <paste deploy.yml>, which token pushes to GHCR, what can it do, and for how long?
Is RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL exposed to pull requests from forks? What would happen if someone pushed a
tag from a fork?
```
**Verify the output by:** reading the GitHub docs pages "Automatic token authentication" and "Using secrets
in GitHub Actions" (secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forks), and checking that
`packages: write` appears only on the image job.

### Prompt 3: Cold start troubleshooting
```text
My container works locally but on Render /health times out for the first minute after idle, then works.
Explain cold starts on free tiers, what my smoke test should do about it, and how to tell a cold start
apart from a crash in the logs.
```
**Verify the output by:** reading your service's Render logs for the boot sequence (migrations applied,
listening on port) and timing `curl -w '%{time_total}' $URL/health` after 20 minutes idle.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] `tracks/<track>/Dockerfile` (multi-stage, non-root, HEALTHCHECK).
- [ ] `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait` + `scripts/smoke-test.sh`: all checks pass,
  and `EXPECT_FALLBACK=true` passes with an unreachable LLM.
- [ ] CI `docker` job green; `deploy.yml` pushed images to GHCR for tag `v1.0.0`.
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` with `[1.0.0]`; `docs/runbook.md` with start/stop/rollback/rotate-secret steps.
- [ ] Optional: a live URL in your README and a green `render` job.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Why do the Dockerfiles copy the dependency manifest before the source code?
- [ ] Docker requires that order
- [x] So that the dependency layer is cached and only rebuilt when the manifest changes
- [ ] To make the image smaller
- [ ] To run tests faster
> **Answer:** Layers are cached top-down; anything after a changed layer is rebuilt. Source changes often, dependencies rarely.

### Q2. Inside Docker Compose, which `DATABASE_URL` host does the app use?
- [ ] `localhost`
- [x] `postgres` (the service name)
- [ ] `127.0.0.1`
- [ ] `host.docker.internal`
> **Answer:** Each container has its own `localhost`. Compose gives services DNS names on a shared network.

### Q3. Why does the image push use `${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER,,}`?
- [ ] To hide the owner name
- [x] GHCR image names must be lower-case and the org name `AICanCode-org` has capitals
- [ ] It is required by Render
- [ ] To support forks only
> **Answer:** `,,` is bash's lower-case expansion. `ghcr.io/AICanCode-org/...` would be rejected.

### Q4. A fork has no `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` secret. What does the `render` job do on a tag push?
- [ ] Fails the workflow
- [ ] Deploys to a default account
- [x] Prints a notice and succeeds; the image is still pushed to the fork's GHCR
- [ ] Waits for someone to add the secret
> **Answer:** Optional infrastructure must not make the pipeline red. Secrets are read into `env:` and tested with `if: env.X == ''`.

### Q5. Why are free hosting instances slow on the first request after a while?
- [ ] The database is re-created
- [x] Idle instances are stopped to save cost and must boot again (cold start)
- [ ] The image is rebuilt
- [ ] DNS caching
> **Answer:** That is why the deploy job polls `/health` for up to 10 minutes before smoke-testing.

### Q6. Why must a deployment never use the `JWT_SECRET` from `docker-compose.yml`?
- [ ] It is too short
- [x] It is public in the repository, so anyone could sign a valid ADMIN token for your API
- [ ] Render rejects it
- [ ] It expires after 30 days
> **Answer:** Whoever knows an HS256 secret can mint any token. Defaults are for laptops; deployments get their own secret from the host's environment variables.

## 7. What you learned
- Production Dockerfiles: multi-stage, layer caching, non-root, health checks, `.dockerignore`.
- Compose profiles to run any track against the same dependencies with one command.
- Black-box smoke tests that work for any implementation of a contract.
- Image builds with layer caching in CI, and delivery to GHCR with the built-in token on version tags.
- Optional, secret-gated deployment that degrades gracefully, plus free-tier trade-offs (cold starts, TLS URLs).
- Semantic versioning and a CHANGELOG-driven release.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-7 phase-6-end          # == v1.0.0
git checkout phase-6-end -- tracks/<track>/Dockerfile docker-compose.yml scripts/smoke-test.sh
git checkout phase-6-end -- .github/workflows/deploy.yml
```

steps.title: Phase 7 · Observability and maintenance (v1.1.0)
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
Shipping v1.0.0 is the start, not the end. In production you have to answer "is it working right now,
and if not, why?" without attaching a debugger. That needs three things: **logs** you can search,
**metrics** you can graph, and a **request ID** that ties a reader's complaint to log lines. DevBlog
also depends on something you do not control, an LLM, so you will run a **game day** where the LLM
hangs, measure what readers feel, and fix it with a **circuit breaker**. Finally you make your
first **maintenance change**, a schema migration plus a backward-compatible API field, and release it
safely as v1.1.0.

## 2. Objectives
- Give every request an `X-Request-ID` (reuse a safe incoming one, or generate a UUID) and put it in every log line.
- Emit structured **JSON logs**: one object per line, one access-log line per request.
- Expose `/metrics` in Prometheus text format with seven counters that are identical in every track.
- Run a **game day**: make the LLM hang, measure comment latency, write a short blameless post-mortem.
- Add an LLM **circuit breaker** (3 failures in a row → open for 30 s → one half-open trial).
- Ship a backward-compatible change: `V2__post_cover_image.sql` + `coverImageUrl` in the API, OpenAPI 1.1.0, CHANGELOG, tag `v1.1.0`.
- Review and merge one Dependabot PR.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 7.1 · Request IDs
Rule (shared by all tracks): if the incoming `X-Request-ID` matches `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$`, echo it;
otherwise generate a UUID. Never echo arbitrary input: a header containing a newline could inject
fake log lines or headers.

<!-- track:java -->
A `OncePerRequestFilter` (`web/RequestIdFilter.java`) sets the response header, puts `requestId` in
the SLF4J **MDC** (so every log line in that request carries it) and logs one `devblog.access` line
with `method`, `path`, `status` and `durationMs` using the fluent API
`LOG.atInfo().addKeyValue("status", …).log()`. `@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)` makes it the first
filter, so even a `401` or a `404` gets an ID (there is no Spring Security filter chain, see ADR-0005).
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
A Starlette middleware (`app/observability.py`) stores the ID in `request.state`, sets the response
header and logs one `devblog.access` record with `extra={"fields": {...}}`. The middleware wraps the
whole app, so error responses (`400`, `401`, `404`) carry the header too.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
Fastify has request IDs built in: `genReqId` (calling `incomingOrNewId()` from `src/observability.ts`)
with `requestIdHeader: false`, so we validate the incoming value ourselves, and a `LogController` with `requestIdLogLabel: "requestId"`.
An `onSend` hook copies `request.id` into the `X-Request-ID` response header.
<!-- /track -->

### Step 7.2 · JSON logs
<!-- track:java -->
One property: `logging.structured.format.console=logstash` in `application.properties`. MDC values
and key/value pairs become JSON fields.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
A small `logging.Formatter` subclass (`JsonFormatter`) that `json.dumps` `ts`, `level`, `logger`, `msg`
and the `fields`; installed by `configure_logging()` at startup.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
Nothing to add: Fastify's logger (pino) already writes JSON, one line per event (`incoming request`,
`request completed` with `responseTime`).
<!-- /track -->

**Never log secrets.** Passwords, access tokens, refresh tokens and the `Authorization` header must not
appear in any log line. Grep for them after the smoke test (`docker compose logs app-<track> | grep -i bearer`
must print nothing).

Check it:
```bash
docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait
curl -s -H 'X-Request-ID: demo-123' localhost:8080/health -o /dev/null -D - | grep -i x-request-id
docker compose logs app-<track> | grep demo-123
```

### Step 7.3 · `/metrics`
Seven counters, same names in all tracks (see `GET /metrics` in `spec/openapi.yaml`):

| Counter | Incremented when |
|---|---|
| `devblog_users_registered_total` | a registration succeeds |
| `devblog_logins_failed_total` | a login is rejected (watch it for credential stuffing) |
| `devblog_posts_published_total` | a post becomes `published` |
| `devblog_comments_created_total` | a comment is stored |
| `devblog_comments_held_total` | moderation holds a comment for review |
| `devblog_ai_fallback_total` | an AI call fell back to the offline rules/template |
| `devblog_llm_short_circuits_total` | the circuit breaker skipped an LLM call (Step 7.5) |

They are hand-rolled on purpose: the Prometheus text format is just
```text
# HELP devblog_logins_failed_total Login attempts answered with 401.
# TYPE devblog_logins_failed_total counter
devblog_logins_failed_total 3
```
In a bigger service you would use Micrometer (Java), `prometheus-client` (Python) or `prom-client` (Node).
`/metrics` is public in this course project; in production you would restrict it to the scraper's network.

### Step 7.4 · Game day: the LLM hangs
A dead LLM is easy: the connection is refused and the fallback answers in milliseconds. A **hanging** LLM
is worse: it accepts the connection and never answers, so every request that needs it waits for the full
`LLM_TIMEOUT_MS` (5 s by default). That is what an overloaded hosted model or a stuck local Ollama looks like.
1. Start the stack at v1.0.0: `git switch --detach v1.0.0`, `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait`.
2. Get the script from the reference: `git show phase-7-end:scripts/game-day.sh > /tmp/game-day.sh && chmod +x /tmp/game-day.sh`,
   then `/tmp/game-day.sh <track>`. It creates a published post and a reader, then runs four phases of
   10 comments each: **offline** baseline, a **healthy** fake LLM, the fake LLM **hanging**, and the LLM
   **back**. The fake LLM is a 15-line Python HTTP server in a throw-away container on the Compose network
   (`MODE=ok` answers like `/v1/chat/completions`, `MODE=hang` never answers), so no model download and no API key.
3. Write down for each phase: status codes, average and maximum latency, the moderation `provider` and
   `fallback` flag, the warnings in the logs, and (from v1.1) the counters. Is any comment lost? Is any
   comment slow? What would 50 comments a minute feel like?
4. Write `docs/postmortem-<date>-llm-hang.md`: summary, impact, timeline, root cause, what went well,
   what to improve, action items. Blameless: describe systems, not people. Read the reference
   post-mortem **after** writing yours (`git show phase-7-end:docs/postmortem-2026-10-02-llm-hang.md`).

### Step 7.5 · Fix: an LLM circuit breaker
Wrap the one LLM client (shared by moderation and summaries) in a `CircuitBreaker`:
- **CLOSED:** calls go through. 3 failures **in a row** open the circuit.
- **OPEN:** calls fail immediately (the caller uses its offline fallback) for 30 s, and
  `devblog_llm_short_circuits_total` is incremented.
- **HALF-OPEN:** after the cooldown, exactly **one** trial call goes through. Success closes the circuit;
  failure re-opens it for another 30 s.

Test it with a fake clock and a fake client (no sleeping in tests): 3 failures → the 4th call does not reach
the client; advance the clock 30 s → one trial; a concurrent second call during the trial is short-circuited.

<!-- track:java -->
`ai/CircuitBreaker.java` implements `LlmClient`, so `AppConfig` wraps the HTTP client once and both
`LlmModerator` and `LlmSummarizer` receive the wrapped instance. State changes are `synchronized`;
the slow HTTP call happens **outside** the lock.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
`CircuitBreaker` in `app/ai.py` has the same `chat()` signature as the HTTP client, a `threading.Lock`
around state changes and `time.monotonic` as the default clock (wall-clock time can jump).
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
`CircuitBreaker` in `src/ai.ts` wraps the client's `chat()`. Node is single-threaded, but `await` still
interleaves requests, so the `trialRunning` flag matters exactly as it does in Java and Python.
<!-- /track -->

Re-run the game day on your branch: in the *hang* phase the first 3 comments still wait for the timeout,
the rest answer in milliseconds with `fallback: true`. In the *back* phase the circuit stays open until the
30 s cooldown has passed, then one trial call closes it again.

### Step 7.6 · Maintenance change: `coverImageUrl` (v1.1.0)
1. `spec/db/migrations/V2__post_cover_image.sql`: `ALTER TABLE posts ADD COLUMN cover_image_url VARCHAR(2048);`
   Nullable, no default, so v1.0.0 code keeps working against the new schema.
2. `CreatePostRequest` / `UpdatePostRequest` accept an **optional** `coverImageUrl`: an absolute `http(s)` URL
   (validated with the regex in the OpenAPI spec; `javascript:` URLs are rejected), `null` clears it.
3. `Post` and `PostListItem` gain `coverImageUrl` (null when not set). Adding a field is backward compatible;
   removing or renaming one is not.
4. `spec/openapi.yaml` → `version: 1.1.0`; `CHANGELOG.md` → `## [1.1.0]`; bump the track's version.
5. Tests first: validation tests for the URL, an API test that sets and clears it, an integration test that
   the column round-trips.
6. Release: `git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "DevBlog v1.1.0" && git push origin main --follow-tags`.
   `deploy.yml` publishes `:1.1.0` and moves `:latest`.

### Step 7.7 · Merge a Dependabot PR
Pick one grouped update. Read its release notes, check that CI is green **including integration tests**,
run it locally if it is a major version, then merge. Write down in `AI_LOG.md` or the PR what you checked.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Structured logging setup
```text
In <Spring Boot 4 | FastAPI | Fastify 5> I want one JSON log line per request with requestId, method,
path, status and durationMs, where requestId comes from a validated X-Request-ID header or a new UUID
and appears on every log line of that request, including 401 responses from the auth layer. Show the
minimal code with no new dependencies, and explain how the request ID is propagated (MDC / contextvars /
child logger). Passwords and tokens must never be logged.
```
**Verify the output by:** sending a request with `X-Request-ID: demo-123` and with a malicious value
(`$'bad\nInjected: 1'` in bash). The first must be echoed and logged, the second replaced by a UUID.
Check `docker compose logs` shows valid JSON (`| jq .`) and that `grep -i bearer` finds nothing.

### Prompt 2: Review my circuit breaker
```text
Here is my LLM circuit breaker in <language>: <paste>. Rules: 3 consecutive failures open it for 30 s,
then exactly one half-open trial; success closes, failure re-opens. Find race conditions (two requests
during the trial), places where the slow call happens while holding a lock, and missing tests. Suggest
tests that use a fake clock instead of sleeping.
```
**Verify the output by:** running the suggested tests and the game day. The short-circuit counter in
`/metrics` must grow by one for every comment after the third in the *hang* phase.

### Prompt 3: Is this migration backward compatible?
```text
I run several app instances and deploy one at a time. Is this migration safe to apply while the old
version is still serving traffic? <paste V2 SQL> What would make it unsafe (NOT NULL, defaults on big
tables, renames)? How would I roll it back?
```
**Verify the output by:** running the **v1.0.0** image against a database that already has V2 applied
(`git switch --detach v1.0.0`, `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build`) and running the v1.0.0
smoke test: it must still pass.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] `X-Request-ID` echoed/generated; JSON access logs visible in `docker compose logs`, no tokens in them.
- [ ] `/metrics` with the seven counters; the v1.1 smoke test passes (57 checks).
- [ ] `docs/postmortem-…-llm-hang.md` with real numbers from your game day.
- [ ] Circuit breaker with fake-clock tests; the game day re-run shows fast fallbacks after 3 failures.
- [ ] `V2__post_cover_image.sql`, `coverImageUrl` in the API, OpenAPI 1.1.0, CHANGELOG, tag `v1.1.0`.
- [ ] One merged Dependabot PR.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Why validate an incoming `X-Request-ID` before echoing it?
- [ ] To make IDs shorter
- [x] An unvalidated value could inject newlines or fake fields into logs and headers
- [ ] Browsers reject long headers
- [ ] UUIDs are faster to generate
> **Answer:** Treat every header as untrusted input. A strict allow-list regex is the simplest defence.

### Q2. During the game day every comment still returned 201. Why is a hanging LLM still an incident?
- [ ] Comments were lost
- [x] Every comment waited for the full LLM timeout, so writers felt seconds of latency and server threads/connections were tied up
- [ ] The database went down
- [ ] Moderation stopped working entirely
> **Answer:** Graceful degradation kept correctness (the rules fallback answered) but not latency. Availability is also about how long users wait.

### Q3. What does the circuit breaker do in the OPEN state?
- [ ] Retries the LLM three times
- [ ] Returns 503 to the client
- [x] Skips the LLM call immediately so the caller uses its offline fallback, until the cooldown ends
- [ ] Switches to a different LLM provider
> **Answer:** It turns a slow failure into a fast one. After the cooldown one half-open trial checks whether the LLM has recovered.

### Q4. Why is `ADD COLUMN cover_image_url VARCHAR(2048)` (nullable, no default) the safe choice?
- [ ] Postgres does not support `NOT NULL` columns
- [x] v1.0.0 code that does not know the column keeps working, and the change is instant
- [ ] It saves disk space
- [ ] It makes the column indexed
> **Answer:** Expand first, (optionally) contract later. A `NOT NULL` column would break inserts from v1.0.0 during a rolling deploy.

### Q5. Adding `coverImageUrl` to the response is a … change.
- [ ] Major (breaking)
- [x] Minor (backward-compatible feature), so 1.0.0 → 1.1.0
- [ ] Patch (bug fix)
- [ ] No version change needed
> **Answer:** SemVer: new optional fields are minor. Removing or renaming a field would be major (2.0.0).

### Q6. Which metric would you alert on to spot a credential-stuffing attack?
- [ ] `devblog_users_registered_total`
- [x] A sudden rise in `devblog_logins_failed_total`
- [ ] `devblog_comments_held_total`
- [ ] `devblog_llm_short_circuits_total`
> **Answer:** Many rejected logins in a short time is the classic signal. The fix (rate limiting per IP/account) is listed as a gap in Phase 8.

### Q7. What makes a post-mortem "blameless"?
- [ ] Nobody writes it
- [ ] It omits the root cause
- [x] It focuses on how the system and process allowed the failure, not on who made a mistake
- [ ] It is kept private
> **Answer:** People hide problems when they fear blame. Blameless reviews produce better action items.

## 7. What you learned
- Correlation IDs, MDC/context propagation and structured JSON logs without secrets.
- Prometheus counters and the text exposition format.
- Game days, blameless post-mortems, and why "hangs" is worse than "down".
- The circuit-breaker pattern, tested with a fake clock.
- Expand-style, backward-compatible migrations and SemVer minor releases.
- Dependency maintenance with Dependabot, and the role of CI as the safety net.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-8 phase-7-end          # == v1.1.0
git diff v1.0.0 v1.1.0 --stat                 # the whole maintenance change
git diff v1.0.0 v1.1.0 -- spec/               # contract + migration only
```

steps.title: Phase 8 · Retrospective and portfolio
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
A recruiter spends about a minute on your repository. "Another blog API" is forgettable; a README that
tells the story (the problem, the security design, the trade-offs, the evidence, what you would do next)
is proof that you can design, test, ship and operate software, and that you use AI responsibly. The
retrospective is for you: it turns nine phases of experience into lessons you can explain in an interview.

## 2. Objectives
- Rewrite the README top section as a **case study** with real numbers from your project.
- Write a short **retrospective** (what went well, what didn't, what you'd change).
- Summarise your **AI_LOG** into three honest bullet points.
- Prepare a 2-minute walkthrough and answers to the security questions interviewers ask about auth APIs.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 8.1 · Collect your evidence
```bash
git log --oneline | wc -l                       # commits
git tag -l 'v*'                                  # releases
make coverage                                    # coverage % per track
scripts/smoke-test.sh | tail -1                  # e.g. "57 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped"
curl -s localhost:8080/metrics | grep _total     # counters after a demo session
```
Also grab: a screenshot of the CI run graph, the GHCR package page, your game-day numbers and
(optionally) your live URL.

### Step 8.2 · README case study
At the top of `README.md`, before the setup instructions, add a section with:
1. **One-line pitch** and a short `curl` session (register → login → publish → comment).
2. **Problem → solution** in three sentences.
3. **Architecture** (link the Mermaid diagrams) and the **three decisions** you are proudest of, linking
   ADRs (for example refresh-token rotation, keyset pagination, AI that may only *hold* a comment).
4. **Security evidence:** which threats from Phase 1 are covered by which tests (reuse detection, drafts
   are `404`, `role` mass assignment ignored, algorithm pinned).
5. **Quality evidence:** tests, coverage, CI badge, smoke test.
6. **Operations:** health, metrics, request IDs, the game day and its post-mortem.
7. **How I used AI**, with honest examples of accepted and rejected suggestions.
8. **What I'd do next** (rate limiting on login, e-mail verification, OpenTelemetry, a small front end…).

### Step 8.3 · Retrospective (`docs/retrospective.md`)
Use *Start / Stop / Continue* or *What went well / What didn't / What I'd change*. Include one
technical lesson (e.g. a fallback is only graceful if the failure is fast), one process lesson
(test-first with a pending list) and one AI lesson (an assistant confidently produced insecure or
outdated code and a test or the docs caught it).

### Step 8.4 · Practise the walkthrough
Record yourself (2 minutes): problem, architecture diagram, one interesting piece of code (the refresh
rotation is a good one), the test that proves it, the CI run, what you'd do next. Then answer out loud:
- *Why short-lived access tokens **and** refresh tokens?* · *What happens if a refresh token is stolen?*
- *Why is someone else's draft `404` and not `403`?* · *How do you prevent lost updates?*
- *Why keyset pagination?* · *What happens when the LLM hangs?* · *Where did AI help, and where did it mislead you?*

### Step 8.5 · Share it
Pin the repository on your GitHub profile, add the topics `rest-api`, `jwt`, `<your-language>`,
`docker`, `github-actions`, and post the case study (aicancode.org *Build in public*, LinkedIn).

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Draft the case study from evidence
```text
Write a README "case study" section (max 400 words) for my blog REST API project from these facts
ONLY: <paste your evidence: test counts, coverage, ADR titles, threats and the tests that cover them,
metrics, post-mortem summary, AI_LOG highlights>. Use short headings. Do not invent numbers, features
or users. Mark anything you are unsure about with [CHECK].
```
**Verify the output by:** checking every number and claim against your evidence list and deleting
anything you cannot show in the repository. If a claim has no link to a file, test or run, cut it.
Watch for security over-claims ("fully secure", "OWASP compliant"): replace them with the specific
threats you handled.

### Prompt 2: Mock security interview
```text
Act as a backend interviewer who cares about security. Ask me 8 questions about this project, one at a
time, from easy to hard, based on this README, the threat list and the ADRs: <paste>. After each answer,
tell me what a strong answer would add. Start now with question 1.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking its "strong answers" against your ADRs, the OWASP cheat sheets
(JWT, password storage, authorization) and the RFCs (RFC 9457, RFC 6749 §10.4 on refresh tokens). An
interviewer persona can still be wrong about details.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] README case study with real evidence and links.
- [ ] `docs/retrospective.md`.
- [ ] AI usage summary (three bullets) in the README, backed by `AI_LOG.md`.
- [ ] A recorded 2-minute walkthrough (optional, but recommended).

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Which README claim is strongest?
- [ ] "Enterprise-grade, fully secure authentication."
- [ ] "Uses JWT best practices."
- [x] "A stolen, already-used refresh token revokes the whole session family, proven by a test (link) that replays a rotated token."
- [ ] "Built with AI."
> **Answer:** Specific, verifiable, linked. Reviewers trust evidence, not adjectives.

### Q2. What belongs in "What I'd do next"?
- [x] Concrete, prioritised improvements with a reason (e.g. login rate limiting, because `devblog_logins_failed_total` is the only defence against credential stuffing today)
- [ ] Everything that is missing
- [ ] Apologies for unfinished work
- [ ] Nothing, it signals weakness
> **Answer:** Knowing the next steps and why shows judgement, and gives the interviewer something to discuss.

### Q3. How should you describe AI use in your portfolio?
- [ ] Hide it
- [ ] Claim the AI wrote everything
- [x] Honestly, with examples of what you verified, changed and rejected
- [ ] Only mention it if asked
> **Answer:** Responsible AI use is a skill employers look for. Your AI_LOG is the evidence.

### Q4. An interviewer asks "What happens when the LLM hangs?" Which answer is best?
- [ ] "The LLM is a managed service, so it does not hang."
- [ ] "Comments fail until it comes back."
- [x] "Comments are still accepted and moderated by the offline rules; after three timeouts a circuit breaker skips the LLM for 30 s, which I measured in a game day."
- [ ] "I would switch to a bigger model."
> **Answer:** Describe the designed behaviour, how you proved it (tests + game day), and what you learned
> (correct but slow is still an incident, see the reference post-mortem).

### Q5. Which retrospective item is most useful?
- [ ] "Security was hard."
- [x] "Our LLM failure test used a refused connection; next time we also test a hanging endpoint and assert a latency budget."
- [ ] "Everything went well."
- [ ] "The AI made mistakes."
> **Answer:** A good retrospective item names a specific cause and a concrete, testable change.

## 7. What you learned
- Turning a project into a case study backed by evidence, including security evidence.
- Running a retrospective and extracting transferable lessons.
- Communicating trade-offs and AI usage clearly and honestly.
- The full lifecycle: requirements and threats → design → implementation → tests → CI/CD → operations → reflection.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git show phase-8-end:README.md | less           # reference case study
git show phase-8-end:docs/retrospective.md
git diff phase-7-end phase-8-end --stat         # docs only
```
